source: Luchins (1942) Mechanization in problem solving: the effect of Einstellung (water-jar problems); figures as reported by Bilalic et al. 2008
finding: Founding Einstellung study. Five set problems solved by one long method (B-A-2C). Two critical problems also had a shorter method; most people kept the long one. On the extinction problem only the short method worked, and many said it was unsolvable.
numbers: Over 80% did not notice the shorter method on the critical problems. 64% failed the extinction problem. Control group that skipped the set problems: only 5% failed it (Luchins & Luchins 1959). Numbers taken from Bilalic et al. 2008 text, not from Luchins himself.
limits: Original study not opened; counts are second-hand. Participants were not experts; set came from five short practice problems.
agent_relevance: A scaffold that reuses one method across several steps may induce the same set. Doubt should fire when the method stops working, not before (G1).

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts - reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters (Cognitive Psychology 56:73-102)
finding: Design: Saariluoma's smothered-mate idea in a water-jar frame. The 2-solution problem has a familiar 5-move mate and a shorter 3-move mate. The 1-solution problem disables the familiar mate with one piece move. Weaker players given only the 1-solution problem set the difficulty baseline, so the Einstellung effect can be priced in skill units.
numbers: Exp 1, share finding the 3-move mate in the 2-solution problem: Grand Masters 100%, International Masters 50%, Masters 18%, Candidate Masters 0%. All IM, M and CM then solved the 1-solution problem (100%). Weaker control group on the 1-solution problem: Class A 63%, Class B 13%, Class C 0%.
quote: Inflexibility of experts is both reality and myth. But the greater the level of expertise, the more of a myth it becomes.
limits: Chess tactics only. Players recruited from clubs in Oxford, Tuzla and Sarajevo and a Bosnian team championship. Instruction was to find the shortest mate. Group sizes are in the paper's Table 1 and are not restated here.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean test pattern for S6: remove the familiar path and see if the agent finds the better one. If it does, the knowledge was there and the first answer blocked it.

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts - reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters (Cognitive Psychology 56:73-102)
finding: The effect is large: a familiar solution cut expert performance to that of players about 3 SD weaker. International Masters (5 SD above mean) with the familiar path present matched Class A (2 SD) without it; Masters matched Class B; Candidate Masters matched Class C.
numbers: Experiment 1 logistic regression on Elo: B = .013, SE = .005, Z = 8.4, p = .004. Each 100 Elo points fewer cut the odds of finding the short mate by a factor of 3.67. Predicted probability: GM (Elo 2550) .64, IM (2450) .32, Master (2350) .12, Candidate Master (2150) .01.
limits: One position in Exp 1. A panel of 12 experts underestimated the effect.
agent_relevance: Fixation is not only a beginner problem: stronger solvers are less prone but still affected on hard items. Do not assume a strong model is immune.

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts - reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters (Cognitive Psychology 56:73-102)
finding: Experiment 2 repeated this on further problems with a wider skill range. Skill predicted escape from the set. Fixation was strongest on hard items and vanished on an easier item (problem 5): all Candidate Masters found the optimal move there.
numbers: Exp 2, first four problems, mean share finding the optimal move: IM/GM 92%, Master 69%, Candidate Master 35%. Weaker controls on the 1-solution versions: Class A 91%, Class B 66%, Class C 47%. Logistic GEE: B = .006, SE = .0016, Z = 3.72, p = .0002; 100 Elo points fewer cut the odds by a factor of 1.82. Experts had predicted 97%, 89%, 73%.
limits: Problem and order of presentation had no effect (all Z < .5). Boundary: the effect depends on an interaction between player skill and the difficulty of the less obvious solution.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for the agent: the fixation cost shows up when the better route is hard to reach. Cheap problems need no doubt step.

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts - reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters (Cognitive Psychology 56:73-102)
finding: Part of the skill gap is immediate recognition and part is escape. Top players often saw the optimal move at once. When they did not, they still found it later far more often than weaker players.
numbers: Where the optimal move was not seen immediately: IM/GM found it later in every instance on problems 1, 2 and 4; Masters in 13 of 24 instances (54%); Candidate Masters in 11 of 32 (34%).
limits: The two mechanisms, faster retrieval and better double-checking, cannot be fully separated in these data.
agent_relevance: Supports a retry after a first answer only if the retry looks at different features (see a13, a14), not the same ones.

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts - reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters (Cognitive Psychology 56:73-102)
finding: Experiment 3 moved from tactics to strategy. Twelve specialists in one opening line solved a plan problem, then a variant where the plan failed, then a third position where the plan worked again despite the old critical feature. Almost all rejected the correct plan.
numbers: Exp 3: 1 of 5 Grand Masters and none of the other players found the best plan in problem 3. Finders had higher Elo (median 2547) than non-finders (median 2258), Mann-Whitney U = 2, p = .017.
limits: N = 12 only, with a single finder. Shows set can come from a rejected plan, not only from a successful one.
agent_relevance: A rejected operator can stay rejected after conditions change. S6 should log why an operator failed so it can be reconsidered when that reason no longer holds.

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts - reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters (Cognitive Psychology 56:73-102)
finding: Theoretical account. Chunks and templates (Gobet & Simon) mean the familiar solution is retrieved first because it is better indexed in long-term memory. ACT-R (strongest production fires) and instance theory (one stored instance wins the race) predict the same fast, hard-to-avoid retrieval. The three theories agree on the set; they differ on how skill reduces it.
numbers: No new numbers. Saariluoma 1990 exceptions: one master not fixated the first time, and one grandmaster who saw both alternatives.
limits: The theories are not compared head to head. The authors say existing theories can explain the effect after the fact.
agent_relevance: In an LLM the most probable continuation plays the role of the strongest production. More draws help only if draws are not all pulled to the same mode (G6, S3 in SCHEMA).

source: Saariluoma (1990) Apperception and restructuring in chess players' problem solving (Exp 2-3); as reported by Bilalic et al. 2008
finding: First chess Einstellung work. Experiment 2: 10 of 12 players missed the shorter solutions in a 2-solution problem. Experiment 3: with the familiar solution present, optimal choices were rare; with it disabled, most found the optimal one.
numbers: Exp 3, two matched groups of 6: with the familiar solution, 11% of choices were optimal and 67% were the familiar non-optimal one; with it disabled, 69% found the optimal solution.
limits: Second-hand from Bilalic 2008. Bilalic notes flaws: no extinction task, a 'mate as fast as possible' instruction, weak players (only 3 above USCF 2100). Source URL is a placeholder for the book chapter and was not opened.
agent_relevance: Same lesson: always run a control with the tempting path removed to tell fixation from lack of knowledge.

source: Wiley (1998) Expertise as mental set: the effects of domain knowledge in creative problem solving (Remote Associates Test with baseball experts); as reported by Bilalic et al. 2008
finding: Domain knowledge can mislead. Participants with more baseball knowledge did worse on misleading Remote Associates items whose cues pointed to baseball answers.
numbers: No figures given in Bilalic's summary.
limits: Second-hand. Bilalic argues this is knowledge from one domain misfiring in a task where it is not expertise.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of a strongly related but wrong frame is also an LLM failure mode; checks should come from code, not from the same retrieval.

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones: the mechanism of the pernicious Einstellung (set) effect (Cognition 108:652-661)
finding: Eye tracking in Candidate Masters. Group 2 saw the 2-solution problem. All reported searching for a shorter mate, yet their gaze stayed on squares tied to the smothered mate for the whole trial.
numbers: Exp 1: group 1 (1-solution problem only) all found the 3-move mate in a mean 79 s (SD 25). Group 2 (2-solution problem) all stopped at the smothered mate after a mean 37 s (SD 20), then solved the 1-solution problem in a mean 148 s (SD 90). Square-set by time interaction, group 2: F(5,20) = 0.6, ns; group 1: F(5,20) = 11.9, p < .001, partial eta-squared = .75. Eye tracker 50 Hz; six time intervals per trial.
quote: Having found one solution, expert chess players reported that they were looking for a better one. But their eye movements showed that they continued to look at features of the problem related to the solution they had already thought of.
limits: Small groups (the t(8) test below implies about 10 players across the two groups). Gaze is a proxy for attention. Players did spend some time on the optimal squares but did not use them.
agent_relevance: Reported search and actual search can differ. An agent's statement that it is 'looking for alternatives' is not evidence; use code to check that new attempts differ from the first (G10).

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones: the mechanism of the pernicious Einstellung (set) effect (Cognition 108:652-661)
finding: Experiment 2: the effect persists after the familiar solution is removed. Players who first met the 2-solution problem took about twice as long on the 1-solution problem as fresh players of the same skill.
numbers: Exp 2 vs the Exp 1 sub-group: t(44) = 2.16, p = .036, d = .65. Skill by group interaction F(2,40) = 0.9, p > .40. Within Exp 1, group 2 vs group 1 on 1-solution time: t(8) = 1.67, p = .13, d = 1.2 (not significant).
limits: Between-experiment comparison. Interpreted by the authors as a decaying priming effect.
agent_relevance: Carry-over: context left by a tempting first attempt slows later attempts. Supports fresh context per attempt (S3).

source: Sheridan & Reingold (2013) The mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: evidence from eye movements (PLoS ONE 8:e75796)
finding: Eye-tracking replication with 17 experts and 17 novices on four problems. In one the familiar move is good but suboptimal; in three it is a blunder. Boundary condition: if the familiar move is a blunder, the set largely vanishes.
numbers: N = 34 (17 experts, mean CFC rating 2223, range 1876-2580; 17 unrated club novices). Problem 1 (advantageous but suboptimal move): 8 of 17 experts and 8 of 17 novices chose the Einstellung move. Problems 2-4 (blunder): all experts and most novices avoided it. Expert move quality higher than novice: t(32) = 6.04 (expert ratings) and 4.93 (engine scores), both p < .001.
limits: Novices fixated in equal proportion, unlike Bilalic where skill mattered. Move-choice task with a 3 minute limit, not 'shortest mate'. Different problems.
agent_relevance: Set strength depends on how good the familiar answer looks. A first answer that passes plausibility checks is the dangerous one; obviously bad ones get dropped.

source: Sheridan & Reingold (2013) The mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: evidence from eye movements (PLoS ONE 8:e75796)
finding: Gaze separates experts who escape from those who do not. Experts who chose the optimal move gradually looked away from the Einstellung move. Experts and novices who chose the Einstellung move kept looking at it. Optimal-choosing experts also made more dwells.
numbers: Problem 1 looking-time linear trend: experts F(1,66) = 13.12, p < .01; novices F(1,66) = 2.25, p = .138. Expertise x time F(3,96) = 3.95, p < .05. Optimal-move experts vs Einstellung-move experts F(3,45) = 3.65, p < .05. Dwells: optimal experts higher than Einstellung experts F(1,15) = 12.34, p < .01. Blunder problems: linear trend experts F(1,66) = 79.88, p < .001; novices F(1,66) = 10.84, p < .01; no group interaction F(3,96) = 1.80, p = .152.
limits: Subgroups of 8 or 9 players. Looking time alone is ambiguous, so the authors add dwell counts.
agent_relevance: A signal that predicts escape: revisiting with new look-ups rather than longer staring at the old ones. Maps to checking whether a retry touches new evidence.

source: Sheridan & Reingold (2013) The mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: evidence from eye movements (PLoS ONE 8:e75796)
finding: Retrospective reports line up with the gaze. Most players said they considered the Einstellung move first. The nine experts who chose the optimal move said they ruled out checkmate in the target region before looking elsewhere.
numbers: Of 8 experts and 8 novices who picked the suboptimal move, 2 experts and 4 novices did not rule out checkmate there (wrongly thought it mated). Blunder moves were ruled out more easily than the suboptimal one.
limits: Verbal reports are retrospective. Small N.
agent_relevance: What distinguishes the escape is an explicit refutation of the first idea. A step that demands a concrete disproof of the first answer is the operational version (S5 REVISE).

source: Ellis & Reingold (2014) The Einstellung effect in anagram problem solving: evidence from eye movements (Front Psychol 5:679)
finding: Einstellung in a simple anagram task (60 undergraduates, 72 trials). A central three-letter string was a word or a scrambled nonword. Familiar words slowed solution. Eye movements show two sides: easier encoding of the word, harder integration of the extra letters.
numbers: N = 60. Accuracy 51.7% word vs 53.8% nonword (t(59) = 1.52, ns). Mean RT 15.3 s vs 13.4 s (t(59) = 3.25, p < .01). Dwells on central string 8.11 vs 6.76 (t(59) = 4.69, p < .001); dwells on single letters 10.45 vs 8.53 (t(59) = 4.80, p < .001). Initial latency on central string shorter for words F(1,59) = 29.78, p < .001; dwell on single letters longer for words F(1,59) = 25.31, p < .001. Overall 52.7% correct, 4.2% wrong, 43.1% timed out (45 s limit).
limits: Not experts: familiarity is word frequency, not training. Accuracy gap not significant, only speed. Pop-out (insight) reports did not differ by condition (68.9% vs 69.2%).
agent_relevance: Familiarity of a chunk makes it harder to split and recombine. Chunk-level tokens (a code idiom, a known puzzle type) may resist O6 representation change.

source: Pope-Caldwell & Washburn (2022) Overcoming cognitive set bias requires more than seeing an alternative strategy (Sci Rep 12:2179)
finding: Competing explanation of set: not 'not seeing' but 'not trying'. In a learned-strategy vs direct-strategy task with eye tracking, people looked at the shortcut location yet did not use it.
numbers: N = 67 undergraduates (91% female). First block: 89.6% did not adopt the shortcut; mean shortcut use 9.56% (SD 25.39%) of correct probe trials; 7 of 67 (10.45%) used it on over half of probe trials. Fixation on the shortcut location higher on probe than base trials: mu = 0.53 (CI .34-.72).
quote: We suggest that cognitive set in the LS-DS task does not stem from an inability to see the shortcut but rather a failure to try it.
limits: Contradicts the attention-capture reading from chess. Authors suggest the shortcut was very salient here, whereas in chess and arithmetic tasks the alternative was not, so the two readings cannot be separated there. Fixation is only a proxy for attention.
agent_relevance: Two failure types need different fixes: unseen alternatives (widen search, O6) and seen but untried alternatives (force a trial of a named alternative, as S6 does by making an operator a subgoal).

source: Pope-Caldwell & Washburn (2022) Overcoming cognitive set bias requires more than seeing an alternative strategy (Sci Rep 12:2179)
finding: Telling people about the better strategy helps most, but not all. After a video of the shortcut, 70.6% of the informed group used it on most trials versus 9.1% of controls who saw the learned strategy.
numbers: Informed N = 34, Controls N = 33. Post-video shortcut use: Informed mean 65.25% (SD 42.88%), Controls 9.12% (SD 25.13%); 24 of 34 informed (70.59%) used it on over 50% of correct trials, 3 of 33 controls (9.09%). 10 of 34 informed (29.41%) still did not adopt it (mean 0.85% use). Valuing the shortcut correlated with use after the video r(67) = .45, p < .001; before it r = .19, ns.
limits: Single task, mostly female undergraduates, optional-switch setting (the learned strategy still works).
agent_relevance: Showing an alternative is not enough; the agent must be made to run it and compare. About a third resisted even when shown.

source: Ninomiya, Terai & Miwa (2022) Differences in the distribution of attention to trained procedure between finders and non-finders of the alternative better procedure (Front Psychol 13:934029)
finding: Who escapes the set? In a water-jar task, finders of the better procedure already spent more attention on information unrelated to the trained procedure while the trained procedure was still working. The difference was absent in the first set trial and grew through repetition.
numbers: 60 recruited, 46 analysed. 67% (31 of 46) found the alternative procedure before the last critical trial. Excluded: 1 discontinued, 4 who did not answer immediately when they found the alternative, 9 who found the alternative on the first critical trial. No difference in attention distribution on the first set trial (equivalence supported).
limits: Eye tracking proxies attention. Japanese undergraduates; water-jar variant. Finders defined after the fact.
agent_relevance: A small amount of attention to off-procedure information during routine success predicts later flexibility. Keep a cheap side-channel that logs unexplained observations even when the main route works.

source: Hatano & Inagaki (1984) Two courses of expertise (Hokkaido Univ. bulletin; earlier version of the 1986 chapter)
finding: Founding distinction. Routine experts are fast, accurate and automatic but cannot handle new problems. Adaptive experts also understand why the procedure works (conceptual knowledge) and can invent or modify procedures. Conceptual knowledge comes from varying the procedure and observing outcomes, plus a tentative model of the domain.
numbers: No experiment numbers in this paper; conceptual claims. Examples: abacus experts, farmers, home cooks.
quote: routine experts are outstanding in terms of speed, accuracy, and automaticity of performance, but lack flexibility and adaptability to new problems
limits: Theory paper; the authors say the empirical evidence is scanty. The better-known 1986 chapter was not opened.
agent_relevance: Defines the target for S6: not speed on known routines but knowing why a step works, which lets the agent choose or invent a different operator.

source: Hatano & Inagaki (1984) Two courses of expertise (Hokkaido Univ. bulletin; earlier version of the 1986 chapter)
finding: Three conditions proposed to favour the adaptive course: (1) the task environment has built-in randomness so the routine sometimes fails; (2) the context rewards understanding, not only speed; (3) intrinsic motivation to understand. Standardised, automated settings (greenhouse growing, precisely quantified recipes) remove the variation needed to learn why.
numbers: No numbers. Rests on Piaget's idea that varying action and watching outcome builds conceptual knowledge.
limits: Speculative; not tested in this paper. Later work measures adaptive expertise differently.
agent_relevance: Training signal: tasks should include variations where the memorised route fails. A scaffold that never meets failure will not learn operator selection.

source: Schwartz, Bransford & Sears (2005) Efficiency and innovation in transfer (chapter in Mestre, Transfer of learning from a modern multidisciplinary perspective)
finding: Reframe: efficiency and innovation are two dimensions, not ends of one line. Adaptive experts are high on both. Pure efficiency produces functionally fixed behaviour (cites Luchins) and routine experts (Hatano & Inagaki). Optimal adaptability needs balance.
numbers: Innovation test example: after invention-based instruction of a few hours, 34% of high-school students invented a measure of covariance; only 12% of top-20 university students after a full statistics course did (Schwartz & Martin 2004).
limits: Chapter-level synthesis. The 34% vs 12% comparison is between very different populations.
agent_relevance: Two-axis scoring for scaffold evaluation: accuracy on trained problems and success on transfer problems with changed structure.

source: Schwartz, Bransford & Sears (2005) Efficiency and innovation in transfer (chapter in Mestre, Transfer of learning from a modern multidisciplinary perspective)
finding: Efficiency first is less stable. Children who learned fractions with pie wedges were more efficient at first but regressed; those who learned with tiles became both more innovative and more efficient.
numbers: Martin & Schwartz 2004 as described in the chapter: over 50% of pie children who reached the adaptive-expertise quadrant regressed the next day; fewer than 15% of tile children did.
limits: Small classroom study reported inside a review chapter; not a replication.
agent_relevance: Early reliance on one fast representation can lock in. Mixing representations early (O6) may give more stable late performance.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996) Reasoning the fast and frugal way: models of bounded rationality (Psychological Review 103:650-669)
finding: Formal model of an adaptive-toolbox heuristic. Take The Best checks cues in order of validity and stops at the first that discriminates. It was compared with integration algorithms on 83 German cities (which is larger) under varying limited knowledge.
numbers: Table 2, average proportion correct across knowledge levels: Take The Best .658, weighted tallying .658, regression .657, tallying .656, Take The Last .645; Minimalist about 1.1 points below the best. With 100% of cue values known: Take The Best .691, regression .694. Take The Best searched between 2 and 20 cue values.
limits: One environment and one criterion. Models were fit on half the cities and tested on the other half. Secondary reports give slightly different totals for other splits.
agent_relevance: A cheap fixed-order rule can match a full weighted model. Operator choice at S6 may not need a learned policy; a validity ordering can do about as well.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996) Reasoning the fast and frugal way: models of bounded rationality (Psychological Review 103:650-669)
finding: The Take The Last variant retries the cue that discriminated last time. The authors say this search principle has been studied as the Einstellung effect in the water-jar experiments. So in the toolbox view, set is a feature that is useful when problems cluster.
numbers: Take The Last average .645 vs Take The Best .658; faster than the Minimalist. In an early run it exploited a systematic order of test pairs and beat the others by about 10 percentage points, which led the authors to randomise the pairs.
limits: Link to Einstellung is the authors' remark (Luchins & Luchins; physician diagnosis generation, Weber et al. 1993). Works only when consecutive problems share structure.
agent_relevance: Order-by-last-success is a sound default when problems cluster; reset it on a signal that the cluster changed (a failed check).

source: Fenwick et al. (2026) Explaining success in Bayesian reasoning with the adaptive toolbox and expertise (Psychon Bull Rev 33)
finding: Recent proposal tying the adaptive toolbox to expertise: tools are learned, automatised and selected through experience; representations such as natural frequencies are scaffolds that make a tool easier for novices, not the only route to success.
numbers: Cites success rates as low as 4% for standard probability formats in Bayesian reasoning; no new data.
limits: Theoretical/review paper; the tool-selection claim is a research agenda, not a tested model.
agent_relevance: Operator choice (S6) is the toolbox selection problem. The review argues for process tracing of expert-novice differences to find which tool was used, which our logging can supply.

source: Kim, Podlasek, Shidara, Liu, Alaa & Bernardo (2025) Limitations of large language models in clinical problem-solving arising from inflexible reasoning (Sci Rep 15:39426; mARC-QA)
finding: LLM test built on the Einstellung effect (mARC-QA, 100 clinical questions written to resist memorisation). Familiar answer patterns sit beside correct long-tail reasoning. Most models scored below 50%; physicians 66%.
numbers: Best models: DeepSeek-R1 52%, DeepSeek-V3 50%, Gemini 1.5 pro 50%, o1 48%. Several models at or below chance (under 20%). Human mean 66% (SE 5.3 points, five physicians). Medalpaca and Meditron models near 0%. Larger Claude, Gemini and OpenAI models did better; Llama 405b worse than 70b. Models overconfident by Brier score and sample consistency (15 stochastic trials per question). On the human-miss set DeepSeek-R1 was confidently correct on 45% and confidently incorrect on 40%.
limits: Only 100 questions, written by the authors; five physicians. Einstellung is the designers' stated cause; no control separates fixation from plain difficulty. Quantised 405b may explain the Llama result.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a fixation test works on LLMs, with overconfidence on wrong answers. Supports not using model confidence as a doubt trigger (G1, G10).
